solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Vigorously active husband permitted one to enter Air Training Corps

indicators.note: the husband, the permission and the one go inside the corps' initials, as if enlisting

parts.note: the initials of the British cadet organisation
allowed, as in 'let him go'
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An energetic husband is allowed to join the air cadets.
explanation.walkthrough: The Air Training Corps is a British youth organisation for would-be airmen, known by its initials.
explanation.definitionFit: An athletic person is physically fit and energetic, so the adjective suits someone vigorously active.

clue.text: Last seen wandering around university in US city

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit either side of the university letter
letters that wander roam out of their order, so the word last is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone was last spotted roaming near a campus somewhere in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last seen' reads like a missing-person report; 'Last' is just the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Tulsa is a large city in the state of Oklahoma.

clue.text: See wife split pants

definitions.note: British slang adjective meaning rubbish or poor, matching the hyphenated adjective

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
a rent is a tear or split in cloth

explanation.surface: Look: the wife's trousers have torn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers, which fits 'split', but here it is British slang for shoddy, and the answer means cheap and inferior.
explanation.definitionFit: Something low-rent is cheap and second-rate, just as British slang calls poor stuff pants.

clue.text: Seaman's waterproof coat

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sailor, an old slang word for one
second meaning: the black pitch spread on a surface as a waterproof layer

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a sailor's oilskin; instead the coat is a layer of the sticky substance itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor is traditionally called a jack tar, and the same short word names pitch used for sealing roofs and hulls.

clue.text: Bloke on Scottish isle briefly left thicket of brushwood

parts.note: a chap is an informal word for a man

indicators.note: cut short, so the island's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde

explanation.surface: A man on a Scottish island has just left a patch of scrub.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaparral is dense scrub of shrubs and dwarf trees, typical of the dry hills of California.

clue.text: Try new driver — fine at first for this game?

parts.note: to have a go is to make an attempt
a learner driver in Britain shows L-plates

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word fine is taken

parts.note: taken as written; its opening letter is the piece

explanation.surface: A suggestion to test out a new driver club, which is fine for the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' suggests a golf club; here a new driver is a learner, shown by an L-plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf is the sport in which a driver is a club, so the clue points to that game.

clue.text: Lizard George found around rock half-hidden

indicators.note: the name's letters are found surrounding the rest
the first half of the word rock is hidden away, leaving its second half

parts.note: taken as written; only its back half survives

explanation.surface: George discovers a lizard lurking half concealed around a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: A gecko is a small climbing lizard with adhesive toe pads.

clue.text: Liberal invited occasionally during religious season

indicators.note: the picked letters fall within the season's name

parts.note: Lent is the forty days of fasting before Easter

indicators.note: only now and then, so every other letter of invited is used

parts.note: taken as written; its second, fourth and sixth letters are used

explanation.surface: A liberal person received an invitation now and then during Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal here means tolerant and permissive, the sense of being lenient rather than strict.

clue.text: Ventilator black, inferior

parts.note: lower in rank or quality

explanation.surface: A list of a poor ventilator's faults: black and second-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: A blower is a fan or device that pushes air, so it serves as a ventilator.

clue.text: Stress Bill associated with money

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
a cent is a small coin

explanation.surface: Worry about a bill always comes along with money matters.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent is emphasis placed on a syllable, so it is a stress in speech.

clue.text: Beware rocky hollow

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Latin for beware, used in English schoolboy slang as a warning
second meaning: an underground chamber in rock

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cave!' was public-school slang for 'look out', from Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a Latin warning cry and a natural cavity in a hillside or cliff.

clue.text: Mel, also abroad with daughter, did some skiing?

definitions.note: the question mark flags a definition by example: one kind of skiing

indicators.note: far and wide, scattered about, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Mel, also overseas with his daughter, went skiing on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' fits a ski trip but signals the shuffle of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Slalom is downhill racing round gates, so to have slalomed is one particular way of having skied.

clue.text: Aristocratic photographer on main road up mountainous area

parts.note: Lord Snowdon, Antony Armstrong-Jones, was a noted photographer and the Queen's brother-in-law

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reverses the road's letters

parts.note: the A1 is Britain's longest numbered road, its digit read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A titled photographer sets up on a main road through hill country.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 is Britain's Great North Road; the figure 1 stands for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Snowdonia is the mountainous region of north Wales, now a national park.

clue.text: Release brick-building toy around end of August

indicators.note: the toy's name wraps around the single letter

parts.note: Lego is the plastic construction brick toy

indicators.note: just the last letter of the month is used

parts.note: taken as written; only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: A toy brick set is launched at the end of August.
explanation.definitionFit: To let go is to stop holding something, which is releasing it.

clue.text: Novice English composer in middle of Palermo

indicators.note: the composer goes inside those core letters

parts.note: the central three letters of the Sicilian city's seven-letter name
Thomas Arne wrote Rule, Britannia!

explanation.surface: A novice English composer is based in the heart of a Sicilian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English' belongs with 'composer', not to an E piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A learner is a beginner still being taught, so a novice.

clue.text: Australian native sought vacant sleeping-place

parts.note: a roo, short for kangaroo

indicators.note: emptied of its middle, so only the first and last letters of sought remain

parts.note: taken as written; only its outside letters remain

explanation.surface: A kangaroo went looking for an empty place to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is the perch where birds settle to sleep.

clue.text: Very busy period of year without Mike and I

indicators.note: lacking, so the letter for Mike is removed

parts.note: a month is one twelfth of a year
ego is Latin for I, the self

explanation.surface: Someone is too busy for a month away from Mike and me.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike is M in the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the go is an idiom for being constantly active and busy.

clue.text: Flipping hat off, notice flower

indicators.note: flipped over, so the whole string reads backwards

parts.note: a lid is slang for a hat
taken as written
an ad is a notice or advertisement

explanation.surface: Someone tips their hat off and spots a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping hat off' reads like doffing a hat; flipping reverses the whole run of pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The daffodil is a yellow spring bloom, the national flower of Wales.

clue.text: Female is not dim

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial contraction of is not

explanation.surface: A woman who is not stupid, so the clue says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' looks like stupid, but it means barely visible.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint light or sound is weak and hard to make out, which is dim.

clue.text: Portable light for shortening necklace

indicators.note: the light's name is shortened, losing its final letter

parts.note: a torch is the British word for a flashlight

explanation.surface: A torch is needed to shorten a necklace.
explanation.walkthrough: A torch in Britain is a battery flashlight.
explanation.definitionFit: A torc is a rigid twisted neck ring of metal worn by ancient Celts.

clue.text: A Parisian in bar gets serving of drinks

indicators.note: the French word sits inside the bar

parts.note: a rod is a bar of metal or wood
un is French for a

explanation.surface: A Parisian at the bar is handed a serving of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, which fits the drinks, but it is a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A round is one set of drinks bought for everyone in a group.

clue.text: Some citizens ignored flag

indicators.note: only part of the run of letters is taken

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A few citizens paid no attention to the flag.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is a flag, especially one flown by a ship to show its nationality.

clue.text: Young reporter embraces woman's angelic child

indicators.note: holds within, so the possessive sits inside

parts.note: a cub is a trainee journalist
her is the possessive for a woman

explanation.surface: A rookie journalist hugs a woman's sweet child.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is a winged child angel in art, so a sweet little infant.

clue.text: Tea household worker left unfinished

indicators.note: the worker's name is left without its last letter

parts.note: a char is a British cleaning lady

explanation.surface: A cleaner's tea was left half-made.
explanation.walkthrough: A char, or charwoman, is a British word for a cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: Cha is an informal British word for tea, from Chinese.

clue.text: Worry about breaking foot

indicators.note: the word for about breaks into the abbreviation

parts.note: re means concerning

explanation.surface: Anxiety over a broken foot.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret is to be anxious and agitated, the same as to worry.

clue.text: Snake study in vast country not starting

indicators.note: the word for study goes inside the rest
the country's name loses its first letter

parts.note: Canada is the world's second largest country
to con is to study or learn carefully

explanation.surface: A snake research project in a huge country doesn't get going.
explanation.definitionFit: The anaconda is a very large South American constrictor.
